title: What is Python?
overview: Before you write a single line of code, you need to understand what programming really is — and why Python is the best place to start. This lecture answers those questions and gets you running your very first program.

blocks.content: Every app on your phone, every website you visit, every game you play — all of it started as instructions written by a human being.

**Programming** is simply the act of writing those instructions. You write them in a special language that the computer can understand, and the computer follows them precisely — step by step, in order, without skipping a single one.

Here's the interesting thing about computers: they are incredibly fast, but they are also completely literal. They don't guess what you mean. They do exactly what you write — nothing more, nothing less.
That's actually a good thing. It means once you learn to write instructions correctly, you can make the computer do almost anything.

analogy.title: Cooking Recipe
analogy.description: A recipe is a set of instructions a human follows to create food. A program is a set of instructions a computer follows to produce output.
bullets: You follow a list of instructions in a specific order.
Each ingredient serves a purpose in the final dish.
Skip one step and the whole recipe turns out wrong.
analogy.highlightCard: A recipe is a program for your kitchen — steps, inputs, and an output.

visualization.title: Recipe → Program
bullets: A program is a sequence of instructions executed in order.
Ingredients in a recipe become input data in a program.
The finished dish becomes the output your program produces.
visualization.highlightCard: Programs work exactly like recipes — instructions in, result out.

code.code:
print("Chop the onions")
print("Boil the water")
print("Serve the meal")
code.output:
Chop the onions
Boil the water
Serve the meal
highlights: Each print() call is one instruction — like one step in a recipe.
Python reads and runs each line top to bottom.
The output is everything Python displays on the screen.
code.highlightCard: Just like a recipe, your Python program runs each line in order and produces an output.

reflection.question: What is the computer equivalent of a 'recipe step'?
reflection.answer: A single line of code — one instruction for the computer to execute.

blocks.stage1Transition: So how does a computer follow instructions? Let's see the programming equivalent.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how this looks in real Python code.
blocks.takeaway: A computer program is like a recipe — you write the steps, the computer follows them in order, and produces a result. That's all programming is.

blocks.title: Write Your First Instructions
blocks.instructions: Your friend wants to bake a chocolate cake but forgot the steps. Write a Python program that prints three steps of any recipe. Each step on its own line.
blocks.starterCode:
# Print three recipe steps
print("Step 1: ")
print("Step 2: ")
print("Step 3: ")
blocks.solution:
print("Step 1: Preheat oven to 180°C")
print("Step 2: Mix flour, sugar, and cocoa powder")
print("Step 3: Bake for 30 minutes")
blocks.hint: Each print() statement outputs one line. Put your step text inside the quotes.
blocks.expectedOutput:
Step 1: Preheat oven to 180°C
Step 2: Mix flour, sugar, and cocoa powder
Step 3: Bake for 30 minutes

blocks.content: There are hundreds of programming languages out there. So why do we teach Python?
Python was created in 1991 by a Dutch programmer named **Guido van Rossum**. His goal was simple: make a language that feels as close to plain English as possible.
He succeeded. Look at this Python code: `print("Hello")`. Even if you've never programmed before, you can guess what it does. That's the power of Python.

Today, Python is used by:
- **Beginners** learning their first language
- **Scientists** analysing data
- **Engineers** at Google, Netflix, and NASA
- **AI researchers** building machine learning models
Python is the most popular language in the world right now. Once you learn it, you can go literally anywhere.

analogy.title: Swiss Army Knife
analogy.description: A Swiss Army knife does everything — scissors, knife, screwdriver, file. Python works the same way: one language, endless uses.
bullets: One compact tool handles dozens of completely different tasks.
You choose the right blade or tool depending on the job.
No need for a separate kit for every situation you face.
analogy.highlightCard: One tool, infinite uses — that's exactly what Python is.

visualization.title: Python's Many Uses
bullets: Python works for web development, data science, AI, automation, and games.
You pick the right library for the task — just like choosing a blade.
One language gives you access to every field of programming.
visualization.highlightCard: Python is the Swiss Army knife of programming languages.

code.code:
# Python works everywhere
print("Web: Flask, Django")
print("Data: Pandas, NumPy")
print("AI: TensorFlow, PyTorch")
code.output:
Web: Flask, Django
Data: Pandas, NumPy
AI: TensorFlow, PyTorch
highlights: # starts a comment — Python ignores it, it's just for humans to read.
print() displays any message to the screen.
One Python file can demonstrate the language's entire range.
code.highlightCard: Python works the same way across web, data, AI, and automation — one language, everything.

reflection.question: Why is Python considered beginner-friendly?
reflection.answer: Its syntax reads like plain English, so you spend less time fighting the language and more time solving problems.
options: It runs faster than other languages
Its syntax reads like plain English

blocks.title: Explore Python's World
blocks.instructions: A student in your class asked 'What can Python do?' Write a program that prints exactly 4 things Python is used for — one per line.
blocks.starterCode:
# Print 4 uses of Python
print("Python can be used for: ")
blocks.solution:
print("1. Building websites")
print("2. Analysing data")
print("3. Creating AI models")
print("4. Automating tasks")
blocks.hint: Use four separate print() statements. You can use your own examples.
blocks.expectedOutput:
1. Building websites
2. Analysing data
3. Creating AI models
4. Automating tasks

blocks.content: Every programmer's journey begins with the same two words: **Hello, World!**
It's a tradition that dates back to the 1970s. The idea is simple — write the smallest possible program that proves the language is working. Something that shows the computer is alive and listening.
In Python, that program is exactly one line long.
`print()` is a **function**. Functions are pre-built tools that do a specific job. The `print()` function's job is to display whatever you put inside the parentheses.
The text you want to display must be wrapped in **quotation marks** — either single `'...'` or double `"..."`. This tells Python: this is text, not a variable or a command.

blocks.title: Try It — Multiple Lines
blocks.code:
print("My name is Lakshanya")
print("I am learning Python")
print("This is my first program")
blocks.expectedOutput:
My name is Lakshanya
I am learning Python
This is my first program

analogy.title: Megaphone
analogy.description: print() is like a megaphone. Whatever you shout into it, Python broadcasts it to the screen.
bullets: Whatever you shout into it, your voice broadcasts to everyone around.
The louder you speak, the more clearly everyone hears.
Without a megaphone, only you can hear your own voice.
analogy.highlightCard: A megaphone broadcasts your voice — print() broadcasts your output to the screen.

visualization.title: How print() Works
bullets: print() displays whatever is inside its parentheses.
You can print text, numbers, or the result of any calculation.
Without print(), nothing appears on your screen — your code runs silently.
visualization.highlightCard: print() is Python's built-in megaphone — it makes your output visible.

highlights: The text inside quotes is called a string — it's what gets displayed.
print() sends it directly to the screen as output.
Each print() call appears on its own separate line.
code.highlightCard: print() is your first Python tool — whatever you put inside it, Python shows on screen.

reflection.question: What does print() do?
reflection.answer: It displays whatever is inside its parentheses to the screen.

keyTakeaways.text: Programming is writing instructions for a computer to follow, step by step.
Python is a beginner-friendly language that reads like plain English.
Python is used in web development, data science, AI, automation, and much more.
print() is a built-in function that displays text to the screen.
Text inside print() must be wrapped in quotation marks.
Every line of code is one instruction — the computer executes them in order.

quiz.question: What does the print() function do in Python?
quiz.explanation: print() is Python's built-in function for displaying output. Whatever you put inside its parentheses appears on the screen when the program runs.

quiz.question: Which of the following is correct Python code to display your name?
quiz.explanation: Python is case-sensitive, so print must be lowercase. Text values must be enclosed in quotes. print(Lakshanya) without quotes would make Python look for a variable called Lakshanya, not the text itself.

quiz.question: Who created the Python programming language?
quiz.explanation: Python was created by Guido van Rossum in 1991. His goal was to create a language that is easy to read and write, as close to plain English as possible.

quiz.question:
What happens when you run this code?
print("Line 1")
print("Line 2")
options: Both lines are printed on the same line
Line 1 is printed, then Line 2 on a new line
quiz.answer: Line 1 is printed, then Line 2 on a new line
quiz.explanation: Each print() statement outputs its text and then moves to a new line. So two print() calls produce two separate lines of output.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT a common use of Python?
quiz.explanation: Python is used for web development, data science, AI, automation, and more. Microchip design is done with specialised hardware description languages, not Python.

quiz.question: Why must text inside print() be wrapped in quotation marks?
options: It tells Python this is text, not a variable or command
It makes the program run faster
It is optional — just a convention
quiz.answer: It tells Python this is text, not a variable or command
quiz.explanation: Without quotes, Python tries to interpret the word as a variable or function name. Quotes tell Python: treat this as literal text to display.
